source_text: Μακρὸν δ’ ἂν εἴη πάντα ἐπεξιέναι τὰ προφητικὰ καὶ τὰ νομικὰ τὰ δἰ αἰνιγμάτων εἰρημένα ἐπιλεγομένους. σχεδὸν γὰρ ἡ πᾶσα ὧδέ πως θεσπίζεται γραφή. ἀπόχρη δ’, οἶμαι, τῷ γε νοῦν κεκτημένῳ εἰς ἔνδειξιν τοῦ προκειμένου ὀλίγα τινὰ ἐκτεθέντα παραδείγματα. αὐτίκα ὁμολογεῖ τὴν ἐπίκρυψιν ἡ περὶ τὸν νεὼν τὸν παλαιὸν τῶν ἑπτὰ περιβόλων πρός τι ἀναφορὰ παρ’ Ἑβραίοις ἱστορουμένη ἥ τε κατὰ τὸν ποδήρη διασκευή, διὰ ποικίλων τῶν πρὸς τὰ φαινόμενα συμβόλων τὴν ἀπ’ οὐρανοῦ μέχρι γῆς αἰνισσομένη συνθήκην. τό τε κάλυμμα καὶ παραπέτασμα ὑακίνθῳ καὶ πορφύρᾳ κόκκῳ τε καὶ βύσσῳ πεποίκιλτο, ᾐνίττετο δ’ ἄρα, ὡς ἡ τῶν στοιχείων φύσις περιέχει τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν τοῦ θεοῦ· ἐξ ὕδατος μὲν γὰρ ἡ πορφύρα, βύσσος δὲ ἐκ γῆς, ὑάκινθός τε ὡμοίωται ἀέρι ζοφώδης ὤν, ὥσπερ ὁ κόκκος τῷ πυρί. ἀνὰ μέσον δὲ τοῦ καλύμματος καὶ τοῦ παραπετάσματος, ἔνθα τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἐξῆν εἰσιέναι, θυμιατήριον τε ἔκειτο σύμβολον τῆς ἐν μέσῳ τῷ κόσμῳ τῷδε κειμένης γῆς, ἐξ ἧς αἱ ἀναθυμιάσεις. μέσος δὲ καὶ ὁ τόπος ἐκεῖνος τοῦ τε ἐντὸς τοῦ καταπετάσματος, ἔνθα μόνῳ τῷ ἀρχιερεῖ ἐπετέτραπτο ῥηταῖς εἰσιέναι ἡμέραις, καὶ τῆς ἔξωθεν περικειμένης αὐλαίας τῆς πᾶσιν ἀνειμένης Ἑβραίοις· διὸ μεσαίτατον οὐρανοῦ φασι καὶ γῆς· ἄλλοι δὲ κόσμου τοῦ νοητοῦ καὶ τοῦ αἰσθητοῦ λέγουσιν εἶναι σύμβολον. τὸ μὲν οὖν κάλυμμα κώλυμα λαϊκῆς ἀπιστίας ἐπίπροσθε τῶν πέντε τετάνυστο κιόνων, εἶργον τοὺς ἐν τῷ περιβόλῳ. ταύτῃ τοι μυστικώτατα πέντε ἄρτοι πρὸς τοῦ σωτῆρος κατακλῶνται καὶ πληθύνουσι τῷ ὄχλῳ τῶν ἀκροωμένων. πολὺς γὰρ ὁ τοῖς αἰσθητοῖς ὡς μόνοις οὖσι προσανέχων. ἄθρει δὴ περισκοπῶν, φησὶν ὁ Πλάτων, μή τις τῶν ἀμυήτων ἐπακούῃ. εἰσὶ δὲ οὗτοι οἱ οὐδὲν ἄλλο οἰόμενοι εἶναι ἢ οὗ ἂν ἀπρὶξ τοῖν χειροῖν λαβέσθαι δύναιντο, πράξεις δὲ καὶ γενέσεις καὶ πᾶν τὸ ἀόρατον οὐκ ἀποδεχόμενοι ὡς ἐν οὐσίας μέρει· τοιοῦτοι γὰρ οἱ τῇ πεντάδι τῶν αἰσθήσεων προσανέχοντες μόνῃ. ἄβατον δὲ ἀκοαῖς καὶ τοῖς ὁμογενέσιν ἡ νόησις τοῦ θεοῦ. ἐντεῦθεν πρόσωπον εἴρηται τοῦ πατρὸς ὁ υἱός, αἰσθήσεων πεντάδι σαρκοφόρος γενόμενος, ὁ λόγος ὁ τοῦ πατρῴου μηνυτὴς ἰδιώματος. εἰ δὲ ζῶμεν πνεύματι, πνεύματι καὶ στοιχῶμεν. διὰ πίστεως περιπατοῦμεν, οὐ διὰ εἴδους. ὁ καλὸς ἀπόστολος λέγει. ἔνδον μὲν οὖν τοῦ καλύμματος ἱερατικὴ κέκρυπται διακονία καὶ τοὺς ἐν αὐτῇ πονουμένους πολὺ τῶν ἔξω εἴργει. πάλιν τὸ παραπέτασμα τῆς εἰς τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων παρόδου, κίονες τέτταρες αὐτόθι, ἁγίας μήνυμα τετράδος διαθηκῶν παλαιῶν, ἀτὰρ καὶ τὸ τετράγραμμον ὄνομα τὸ μυστικόν, ὃ περιέκειντο οἷς μόνοις τὸ ἄδυτον βάσιμον ἦν· λέγεται δὲ Ἰαουε, ὃ μεθερμηνεύεται ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἐσόμενος. καὶ μὴν καὶ καθ’ Ἕλληνας θεὸς τὸ ὄνομα τετράδα περιέχει γραμμάτων. εἰς δὲ τὸν νοητὸν κόσμον μόνος ὁ κύριος ἀρχιερεὺς γενόμενος εἴσεισι, διὰ τῶν παθῶν εἰς τὴν τοῦ ἀρρήτου γνῶσιν παρεισδυόμενος, ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὄνομα ἐξαναχωρῶν, ὃ φωνῇ γνωρίζεται.
pass_a_gloss: It would be a long task to go through all the prophetic and legal things said through riddles, which are called allegories. For nearly the whole scripture is thus ordained. But I think it is enough for one who has a mind to have a few examples presented as an indication of what is at hand. The covering of the old temple of the Hebrews, with its seven surrounding areas, immediately confesses the symbol of the covenant from heaven to earth, through various symbols of the things that appear. The veil and the curtain, embroidered with hyacinth and purple and scarlet and fine linen, signified, then, that the nature of the elements contains the revelation of God; for the purple is from the water, the fine linen from the earth, and the hyacinth, being dark, is similar to the air, just as the scarlet is to the fire. And in the middle of the veil and the curtain, where the priests were allowed to enter, an altar of incense was placed, a symbol of the earth that lies in the middle of this world, from which the incense offerings arise. And the place is also in the middle, both of the area inside the curtain, where only the high priest was allowed to enter on certain days, and of the outer court that surrounded it, which was open to all Hebrews; therefore, they say it is a symbol of what is between heaven and earth; others say it is a symbol of the intelligible and sensible world. The veil, then, was a barrier to the lack of faith of the people, in addition to the five stretched-out pillars, which kept those in the surrounding area out. In this way, the five loaves of bread are mystically broken by the Savior and multiplied for the crowd of listeners. For many people are inclined towards the sensible things as if they were the only things that exist. 'Gather, then, and examine carefully,' Plato says, 'lest any of the uninitiated hear.' These are the people who think that nothing else exists except what they can grasp with their hands, and who do not accept actions and generations and all invisible things as part of reality; for they are inclined towards the five senses alone. The understanding of God is inaccessible to hearing and to those who are of the same kind. From this, the Son is said to be the face of the Father, having become flesh and having five senses, the Word being the interpreter of the paternal characteristic. If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. We walk by faith, not by sight, the good Apostle says. Inside the veil, then, a priestly ministry is hidden, and it keeps those who are laboring in it much more than those outside. Again, the curtain of the entrance to the holy of holies, with four pillars there, is a holy message of the four old covenants; and also the mystical four-letter name, which was surrounded by those to whom alone the inner sanctuary was accessible; it is called Iaoue, which is translated as 'He who is' and 'He who will be.' And indeed, the name 'God' among the Greeks also contains a tetrad of letters. But into the intelligible world, only the Lord, having become a high priest, will enter, by passing through the passions into the knowledge of the ineffable, going beyond every name that is known by voice.

pass_b_english: To go through every prophetic and legal passage spoken in riddles, which we call allegories, would be a long task; for nearly all Scripture is ordained in this way. I think, however, that a few examples will suffice to show one who has a mind what is at hand. The covering of the old Hebrew temple, with its seven surrounding courts, immediately confesses the symbol of the covenant stretching from heaven to earth through various symbols of the visible world. The veil and the curtain, embroidered with hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, signified that the nature of the elements contains the revelation of God. Purple comes from water, fine linen from the earth; hyacinth, being dark, resembles the air, just as scarlet resembles fire. In the space between the veil and the curtain, where priests were allowed to enter, stood an altar of incense — a symbol of the earth placed in the middle of this world, from which the offerings of incense arise. That place is also midway between the inner sanctuary, where only the high priest could enter on appointed days, and the outer court open to all Hebrews; therefore they say it symbolizes what lies between heaven and earth, while others say it represents the intelligible and the sensible worlds. The veil served as a barrier to the people's unbelief, stretched across five pillars that kept those in the courtyard out. In this very way, the five loaves are mystically broken by the Savior and multiplied for the crowd of listeners. For many attend only to sensible things as if they alone existed. "Gather, then, and examine carefully," says Plato, "lest any of the uninitiated hear." These are the people who think nothing exists except what they can grasp with their hands, refusing to accept actions, generations, and all invisible realities as part of true being; for they incline only to the five senses. The understanding of God is inaccessible to hearing and to those of like kind. From this the Son is called the face of the Father, having become flesh endowed with five senses, the Word who interprets the Father's distinctive character. "If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. We walk by faith, not by sight," the good Apostle says (2 Corinthians 5:7). Inside the veil, then, a priestly ministry is hidden, and it holds those who labor in it far more strictly than those outside. Again, the curtain at the entrance to the holy of holies rests on four pillars — a holy sign of the four ancient covenants — and also of the mystical four-letter name that was guarded by those alone to whom the inner sanctuary was accessible. It is called Iaoue, which translates as "He who is" and "He who will be." And indeed, even among the Greeks the name "God" contains a tetrad of letters. But into the intelligible world only the Lord enters, having become high priest; passing through the passions into the knowledge of the ineffable, he goes beyond every name known by voice.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological and symbolic arguments of the Greek text. Pass A preserves the nuances of the Greek clauses, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that adheres to Pass A and the source. Scripture citations (2 Corinthians 5:7) are correctly identified and added to Pass B as required. The title 'Symbolism in the Temple' correctly names the thought.
